claim: Highly distributed neural circuits are thought to support adaptive decision-making in volatile and complex environments.
source: Highly distributed neural circuits are thought to support adaptive decision-making in volatile and complex environments.
evidence: This is a general statement about neural circuits and decision-making that reflects established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Functional interactions between prefrontal and reciprocally connected thalamic nuclei areas may be important when choices are guided by current goal value or action-outcome contingency.
source: Notably, the functional interactions between prefrontal and reciprocally connected thalamic nuclei areas may be important when choices are guided by current goal value or action-outcome contingency.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential importance of these interactions, indicated by the word 'may'.

claim: Thalamocortical and corticothalamic pathways differentially support goal attributes.
source: Using a chemogenetic approach to inhibit projection-defined dmPFC and MD neurons during an instrumental learning task, we show that thalamocortical and corticothalamic pathways differentially support goal attributes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the chemogenetic inhibition experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Both thalamocortical and corticothalamic pathways participate in adaptation to the current goal value.
source: Both pathways participate in adaptation to the current goal value, but only thalamocortical neurons are required to integrate current causal relationships.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental results from both Experiment 1 and Experiment 2 showing deficits in devaluation tests.

claim: Only thalamocortical neurons are required to integrate current causal relationships.
source: Both pathways participate in adaptation to the current goal value, but only thalamocortical neurons are required to integrate current causal relationships.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing that only thalamocortical pathway inhibition impaired contingency degradation performance.

claim: Antiparallel flow of information within thalamocortical circuits may convey qualitatively distinct aspects of adaptive decision-making.
source: These data indicate that antiparallel flow of information within thalamocortical circuits may convey qualitatively distinct aspects of adaptive decision-making and highlight the importance of the direction of information flow within neural circuits.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects observed when inhibiting thalamocortical versus corticothalamic pathways.

claim: The dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) plays a central role in adaptive decision-making.
source: Past research points to a central role for the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) in adaptive decision-making (Corbit and Balleine, 2003; Killcross and Coutureau, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Areas innervating the PFC play a major role in the circuit-level analysis of the functional role of the PFC.
source: A circuit-level analysis of the functional role of the PFC also indicates a major role for areas innervating the PFC (O'Doherty, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The mediodorsal thalamus (MD) has extensive reciprocal projections connecting with the dmPFC.
source: In this respect, the mediodorsal thalamus (MD) appears of special interest due to the extensive reciprocal projections connecting these two areas (Groenewegen, 1988; Gabbott et al., 2005; Alcaraz et al., 2016a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The role of the thalamus is not limited to that of a relay.
source: These anatomical considerations helped to shape a new functional view of the thalamus, wherein its role is not limited to that of a relay (Sherman, 2005; Mitchell, 2015; Wolff et al., 2015a; Sherman, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Experimental interventions aimed at the MD produce a vast array of specific cognitive deficits on both rodents and primates.
source: Indeed experimental interventions aimed at the MD produce a vast array of specific cognitive deficits on both rodents and primates (Corbit et al., 2003; Baxter, 2013; Parnaudeau et al., 2013; Parnaudeau et al., 2015; Alcaraz et al., 2016b; Chakraborty et al., 2016), supporting the view that this thalamic area plays an integrative role within thalamocortical circuits (Schmitt et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: The mediodorsal thalamus plays an integrative role within thalamocortical circuits.
source: Indeed experimental interventions aimed at the MD produce a vast array of specific cognitive deficits on both rodents and primates (Corbit et al., 2003; Baxter, 2013; Parnaudeau et al., 2013; Parnaudeau et al., 2015; Alcaraz et al., 2016b; Chakraborty et al., 2016), supporting the view that this thalamic area plays an integrative role within thalamocortical circuits (Schmitt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference supported by cited experimental evidence and a citation.

claim: The functional significance of reciprocal projections has not been directly examined in the context of adaptive decision-making.
source: Surprisingly, the functional significance of reciprocal projections, which are the hallmark of thalamocortical organization, has not been directly examined in the context of adaptive decision-making.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, reflecting the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: Thalamocortical and corticothalamic pathways recruited by the same behavioral task may support qualitatively distinct aspects of working memory.
source: A recent report provided initial evidence that thalamocortical and corticothalamic pathways recruited by the same behavioral task may support qualitatively distinct aspects of working memory (Bolkan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Goal-directed actions must classically fulfill two criteria: dependence on current goal value and on the causal link between the action and its outcome.
source: To qualify as 'goal-directed', actions must classically fulfill two criteria: dependence on current goal value and on the causal link between the action and its outcome (Balleine and Dickinson, 1998).
evidence: This is a definition from the field supported by a citation.

claim: An adeno-associated virus carrying a floxed hM4Di receptor expression cassette was injected in the MD to express an inhibitory DREADD receptor only in dmPFC-projecting MD cells.
source: To express an inhibitory DREADD receptor (Armbruster et al., 2007) only in dmPFC-projecting MD cells, an adeno-associated virus carrying a floxed hM4Di receptor expression cassette was injected in the MD, while a retrograde CAV-2 vector (Junyent and Kremer, 2015) carrying the Cre recombinase was injected in the dmPFC (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: A retrograde CAV-2 vector carrying the Cre recombinase was injected in the dmPFC.
source: To express an inhibitory DREADD receptor (Armbruster et al., 2007) only in dmPFC-projecting MD cells, an adeno-associated virus carrying a floxed hM4Di receptor expression cassette was injected in the MD, while a retrograde CAV-2 vector (Junyent and Kremer, 2015) carrying the Cre recombinase was injected in the dmPFC (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Only thalamic cells projecting to the dmPFC were infected by both vectors and therefore expressed mCherry and hM4Di.
source: As a result, only thalamic cells projecting to the dmPFC were infected by both vectors and therefore expressed mCherry and hM4Di.
evidence: This is an inference based on the viral vector strategy employed.

claim: mCherry expression was more evident in the lateral portion of the MD.
source: In general mCherry expression was more evident in the lateral portion of the MD, in agreement with our current knowledge of these thalamocortical projections (Alcaraz et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data that is consistent with cited anatomical knowledge.

claim: mCherry expression was visible to some degree in adjacent dmPFC-projecting thalamic areas such as the intralaminar group (PC and CL mostly) and, to some extent, the CM and the PV.
source: mCherry expression was also visible to some degree in adjacent dmPFC-projecting thalamic areas such as the intralaminar group (PC and CL mostly) and, to some extent, the CM and the PV.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: In some cases, fluorescence was also observed in the habenula.
source: In some cases, fluorescence was also observed in the habenula.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Eight rats showed only minimal (or unilateral) levels of DREADD expression and were therefore excluded from the analyses.
source: Eight rats showed only minimal (or unilateral) levels of DREADD expression and were therefore excluded from the analyses (saline: n = 7, CNO: n = 7).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and data quality control.

claim: Instrumental performance progressively increased over training for both CNO- and saline-treated groups.
source: Instrumental performance progressively increased over training for both CNO- and saline-treated groups, as shown by the significant effect of Session (F(5,60) = 11.7, p<0.0001), but CNO-treated rats tended to perform fewer lever presses overall (F(1,12) = 11.4, p=0.0055) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: CNO-treated rats tended to perform fewer lever presses overall during instrumental training.
source: Instrumental performance progressively increased over training for both CNO- and saline-treated groups, as shown by the significant effect of Session (F(5,60) = 11.7, p<0.0001), but CNO-treated rats tended to perform fewer lever presses overall (F(1,12) = 11.4, p=0.0055) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no significant Drug X Session interaction during instrumental training in Experiment 1.
source: There was no significant Drug X Session interaction however (F < 1), confirming efficient instrumental learning even for the CNO-treated group.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The asymptotical performance did not differ between saline-treated and CNO-treated groups during the final session of training in Experiment 1.
source: In addition, the asymptotical performance did not differ between saline-treated and CNO-treated groups during the final session of training (F(1,12) = 2.58, p=0.1338).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Both groups of rats consumed the same amount of food during devaluation by specific satiety in Experiment 1.
source: During devaluation by specific satiety, both groups of rats consumed the same amount of food (Saline group: 10.8 ± 0.5 g, CNO group: 12.8 ± 0.8 g; F(1,12) = 1.7, p=0.2214), indicating that basic motivational processes were not altered by CNO treatment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Basic motivational processes were not altered by CNO treatment in Experiment 1.
source: During devaluation by specific satiety, both groups of rats consumed the same amount of food (Saline group: 10.8 ± 0.5 g, CNO group: 12.8 ± 0.8 g; F(1,12) = 1.7, p=0.2214), indicating that basic motivational processes were not altered by CNO treatment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the equal food consumption data.

claim: Rats that received saline exhibited a clear bias toward the action associated with the still valued outcome during the devaluation test in Experiment 1.
source: While the group of rats that received saline exhibited the expected adaptive behavior during that test, expressing a clear bias toward the action associated with the still valued outcome, rats that received CNO showed only little differential response toward either actions (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Rats that received CNO showed only little differential response toward either actions during the devaluation test in Experiment 1.
source: While the group of rats that received saline exhibited the expected adaptive behavior during that test, expressing a clear bias toward the action associated with the still valued outcome, rats that received CNO showed only little differential response toward either actions (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The critical Devaluation X Drug interaction approached significance in the devaluation test of Experiment 1.
source: Consistent with these observations, the critical Devaluation X Drug interaction approached significance (F(1,12) = 4.0, p=0.0679), while the main effect of Devaluation (F(1,12) = 10.0, p=0.0081) but not of Drug (F < 1) reached significance.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: A significant effect of Devaluation was evident for the saline group but not the CNO group in Experiment 1.
source: When considering each group separately, a significant effect of Devaluation was evident for the saline (F(1,6) = 7.7, p=0.0324) but not the CNO group (F(1,6) = 2.7, p=0.1543).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Responding gradually decreased over time during the devaluation test for both saline- and CNO-treated groups in Experiment 1.
source: Moreover, analyses conducted on each group separately confirmed that responding gradually decreased over time during this test (Saline: Block, F(4,24) = 6.6, p=0.0010; CNO: Block, F(4,24) = 7.4, p=0.0005).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The impairment in the CNO group during the devaluation test was not the result of a performance deficit.
source: Thus, responding was initially higher and then declined to comparable rates for both saline- and CNO-treated groups suggesting that the impairment in the CNO group was not the result of a performance deficit.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of responding dynamics over time.

claim: The CNO treatment produced a mild deficit in the ability to update goal value representation and/or its use to guide behavior in Experiment 1.
source: Collectively, these data therefore suggest that the CNO treatment produced a mild deficit in the ability to update goal value representation and/or its use to guide behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results from the devaluation test.

claim: Both saline- and CNO-treated rats preferably consumed the still valued outcome when they could freely select from the two outcomes in the consumption test of Experiment 1.
source: That is, both saline- and CNO-treated rats preferably consumed the still valued outcome when they could freely select from the two outcomes (Devaluation (F(1,12) = 25.6, p=0.0003; Drug and Drug X Devaluation, Fs < 1; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The sensory-specific satiety was effective and left unaltered by CNO administration in Experiment 1.
source: Importantly, a consumption test performed immediately after the devaluation test confirmed the effectiveness of the sensory-specific satiety, which was left unaltered by CNO administration.
evidence: This is supported by the consumption test data.

claim: Differential responding was evident for both saline- and CNO-treated groups during the degradation phase in Experiment 1, with lower responding when action-outcome contingency was degraded.
source: During the degradation phase, differential responding was evident for both saline- and CNO-treated groups with lower responding when action-outcome contingency was degraded (Figure 3D), as shown by the significant Degradation effect (F(1,12) = 52.8, p<0.0001) as well as the significant Session X Degradation interaction (F(5,60) = 3.1, p=0.0152).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Drug treatment did not produce any visible effect during the degradation phase in Experiment 1.
source: Drug treatment did not produce any visible effect on this occasion (Drug, F(1,12) = 1.6, p=0.2305; Session x Drug, F(5,60) = 1.6, p=0.1820; all remaining Fs < 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: When the sensory feedback provided by the outcome was available, all rats were capable of exhibiting adaptive decision-making in Experiment 1.
source: Thus, when the sensory feedback provided by the outcome was available, all rats were capable of exhibiting adaptive decision-making, showing that the consequences of their actions strongly affected their behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the degradation phase results.

claim: Saline-treated rats continued to express differential responding for both actions during the final choice test in Experiment 1.
source: While saline-treated rats continued to express differential responding for both actions, CNO-treated rats were unable to do so.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the final choice test.

claim: CNO-treated rats were unable to express differential responding for both actions during the final choice test in Experiment 1.
source: While saline-treated rats continued to express differential responding for both actions, CNO-treated rats were unable to do so.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the final choice test.

claim: The critical Degradation X Drug interaction was significant in the final choice test of Experiment 1.
source: In line with these observations, the critical Degradation X Drug interaction was significant (F(1,12) = 5.6, p=0.0354), as were the main effects of Drug (F(1,12) = 6.8, p=0.0225) and of Degradation (P(1,12) = 6.0, p=0.0310).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The main effect of Degradation was significant for the saline-treated but not the CNO-treated group in the final choice test of Experiment 1.
source: Further analyses confirmed that the main effect of Degradation was significant for the saline-treated (F(1,6) = 12.2, p=0.0129) but not the CNO-treated group (F < 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Neither CNO nor DMSO treatment altered behavior throughout testing in control experiments.
source: We provide as an Appendix supplemental data showing that these effect did not result from CNO alone because neither CNO nor DMSO treatment altered behavior throughout testing (Appendix 1—figures 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by control experiment data provided in the appendix.

claim: Inhibiting dmPFC-projecting MD neurons produced selective impairments when rats were forced to rely on representations to guide behavior.
source: Thus, inhibiting dmPFC-projecting MD neurons produced selective impairments when rats were forced to rely on representations to guide behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of results across different test conditions in Experiment 1.

claim: Thalamocortical pathways play a central role in the ability to guide choice based on current knowledge of the causal link between actions and their outcomes.
source: Overall, these data indicate a central role for thalamocortical pathways in the ability to guide choice based on current knowledge of the causal link between actions and their outcomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overall pattern of results from Experiment 1.

claim: A marked expression of mCherry was evident in deep cortical layers in Experiment 2.
source: A marked expression of mCherry was evident in deep cortical layers, consistent with the existence of abundant corticothalamic projections targeting the MD from cortical layers 5/6 (Gabbott et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data that is consistent with cited anatomical knowledge.

claim: Greater labelling was evident for CT cells compared to TC cells.
source: Although we did not quantify the number of labelled cells, comparing experiments 1 and 2 shows that greater labelling was evident for CT cells, consistent with the view that CT cells outnumber TC cells (eg., Haber and Calzavara, 2009).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the two experiments, supported by a citation.

claim: CT cells outnumber TC cells.
source: Although we did not quantify the number of labelled cells, comparing experiments 1 and 2 shows that greater labelling was evident for CT cells, consistent with the view that CT cells outnumber TC cells (eg., Haber and Calzavara, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Six animals showed little or unilateral DREADD expression and were not considered for analyses in Experiment 2.
source: Six animals showed little or unilateral DREADD expression and were not considered for analyses (saline: n = 8, CNO: n = 6).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and data quality control.

claim: Instrumental learning was comparable between saline- and CNO-treated rats in Experiment 2.
source: Instrumental learning was comparable between saline- and CNO-treated rats (Figure 4A), with improved instrumental learning over training (F(5,12) = 99.3, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Instrumental learning was not affected by CNO in Experiment 2.
source: Instrumental learning was not affected by CNO (Drug, F(1,12) = 3.1, p=0.1050; Session X Drug interaction, F < 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: All rats consumed an equal amount of food during devaluation in Experiment 2, irrespective of whether they were treated with saline or CNO.
source: During devaluation, all rats again consumed an equal amount of food, irrespective of whether they were treated with saline or CNO (Saline group: 9.1 ± 0.6 g, CNO group: 9.1 ± 0.7 g; F < 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The saline group expressed a clear bias for the still valued option during the devaluation test in Experiment 2.
source: Immediately after the devaluation procedure however, the choice test conducted in extinction revealed a markedly distinct pattern of response in the two groups of rats (Figure 4B). While the saline group expressed a clear bias for the still valued option, the CNO group responded similarly for both actions, consistent with the view that they failed to use current goal value to guide behavior.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The CNO group responded similarly for both actions during the devaluation test in Experiment 2.
source: Immediately after the devaluation procedure however, the choice test conducted in extinction revealed a markedly distinct pattern of response in the two groups of rats (Figure 4B). While the saline group expressed a clear bias for the still valued option, the CNO group responded similarly for both actions, consistent with the view that they failed to use current goal value to guide behavior.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CNO-treated rats failed to use current goal value to guide behavior in Experiment 2.
source: Immediately after the devaluation procedure however, the choice test conducted in extinction revealed a markedly distinct pattern of response in the two groups of rats (Figure 4B). While the saline group expressed a clear bias for the still valued option, the CNO group responded similarly for both actions, consistent with the view that they failed to use current goal value to guide behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data from the devaluation test.

claim: The critical Drug X Devaluation interaction reached significance in the devaluation test of Experiment 2.
source: Importantly, the critical Drug X Devaluation interaction reached significance (F(1,12) = 9.2, p=0.0103), providing compelling support for these observations.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: A selective deficit was observed in CNO-treated but not saline-treated rats during the devaluation test in Experiment 2.
source: Separate analyses confirmed the existence of a selective deficit in CNO-treated (Devaluation, F < 1) but not saline-treated (Devaluation, F(1,7) = 23.1, p=0.0020) rats.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Responding decreased over time in a similar fashion for both saline and CNO groups during the devaluation test in Experiment 2.
source: Further analyses confirmed a significant effect of Block for both saline- (F(4,28) = 5.0, p=0.0035) and CNO-treated (F(4,28) = 5.6, p=0.0034) groups suggesting that responding decreased over time in a similar fashion for both groups.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Floor effect alone cannot account for the specific impairment evident during the devaluation test in Experiment 2.
source: Thus, floor effect alone cannot account for the specific impairment evident during this test.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of responding dynamics.

claim: All rats expressed a clear bias for the still valued outcome in the consumption test of Experiment 2.
source: Consumption tests conducted immediately after yielded essentially the same results as in experiment 1: all rats expressed a clear bias for the still valued outcome (the sensory-specific satiety procedure was efficient) and CNO treatment did not alter behavior at this stage (Devaluation, (F(1,12) = 44.0, p<0.0001; Drug, (F(1,12) = 1.9, p=0.1934; Drug X Devaluation, F < 1, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The sensory-specific satiety procedure was efficient in Experiment 2.
source: Consumption tests conducted immediately after yielded essentially the same results as in experiment 1: all rats expressed a clear bias for the still valued outcome (the sensory-specific satiety procedure was efficient) and CNO treatment did not alter behavior at this stage (Devaluation, (F(1,12) = 44.0, p<0.0001; Drug, (F(1,12) = 1.9, p=0.1934; Drug X Devaluation, F < 1, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the consumption test results.

claim: CNO treatment did not alter behavior during the consumption test in Experiment 2.
source: Consumption tests conducted immediately after yielded essentially the same results as in experiment 1: all rats expressed a clear bias for the still valued outcome (the sensory-specific satiety procedure was efficient) and CNO treatment did not alter behavior at this stage (Devaluation, (F(1,12) = 44.0, p<0.0001; Drug, (F(1,12) = 1.9, p=0.1934; Drug X Devaluation, F < 1, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Differential responding was evident for both saline- and CNO-treated groups during the degradation phase in Experiment 2, with lower responding when action-outcome contingency was degraded.
source: Differential responding was evident for both saline- and CNO-treated groups with lower responding when action-outcome contingency was degraded (CNO treatment produced no visible effect, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CNO treatment produced no visible effect during the degradation phase in Experiment 2.
source: Differential responding was evident for both saline- and CNO-treated groups with lower responding when action-outcome contingency was degraded (CNO treatment produced no visible effect, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: All rats continued to select the action with reliable consequences during the final choice test in Experiment 2.
source: During the final choice test conducted in extinction (Figure 4E), all rats continued to select the action with reliable consequences as attested by the significant effect of Degradation (F(1,12) = 5.8, p=0.0331).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Inhibiting corticothalamic pathways produced no noticeable effect during the final choice test in Experiment 2.
source: Importantly, inhibiting corticothalamic pathways produced no noticeable effect and did not prevent rats to display adaptive decision-making even when they could only rely on represented information (Drug and Drug X Degradation, Fs <1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Inhibiting corticothalamic pathways did not prevent rats from displaying adaptive decision-making when they could only rely on represented information.
source: Importantly, inhibiting corticothalamic pathways produced no noticeable effect and did not prevent rats to display adaptive decision-making even when they could only rely on represented information (Drug and Drug X Degradation, Fs <1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results from the final choice test.

claim: Dissociable patterns of performance were obtained when inhibiting thalamocortical and corticothalamic pathways during choice tests conducted under extinction conditions.
source: Thus, dissociable patterns of performance were obtained when inhibiting thalamocortical and corticothalamic pathways during choice tests conducted under extinction conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the results from Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: A clear deficit in the ability to use recently updated goal value was observed when inhibiting the corticothalamic pathway.
source: A clear deficit in the ability to use recently updated goal value was observed when inhibiting the corticothalamic pathway, but the same treatment did not prevent animals to adapt to a selective change in the contingency between an action and its outcome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the results from Experiment 2.

claim: Inhibiting the corticothalamic pathway did not prevent animals from adapting to a selective change in the contingency between an action and its outcome.
source: A clear deficit in the ability to use recently updated goal value was observed when inhibiting the corticothalamic pathway, but the same treatment did not prevent animals to adapt to a selective change in the contingency between an action and its outcome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the results from Experiment 2.

claim: The ability to adapt to a selective change in the contingency between an action and its outcome was abolished by the inhibition of the thalamocortical pathway.
source: The latter ability was however abolished by the inhibition of the thalamocortical pathway, which also produced a mild deficit in the ability to use goal value to guide behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the results from Experiment 1.

claim: Inhibition of the thalamocortical pathway produced a mild deficit in the ability to use goal value to guide behavior.
source: The latter ability was however abolished by the inhibition of the thalamocortical pathway, which also produced a mild deficit in the ability to use goal value to guide behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the results from Experiment 1.

claim: Both cortical and thalamic neurons contribute importantly to the ability to perform adaptive actions.
source: The present data indicate an important contribution for both cortical and thalamic neurons in the ability to perform adaptive actions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overall results from both experiments.

claim: Both cortical and thalamic neuronal populations were found to be important to guide behavior based on current goal value.
source: However, while both neuronal populations were found to be important to guide behavior based on current goal value, only thalamic neurons critically supported choice based on current causal relationships.
evidence: This is an inference based on the results from both experiments.

claim: Only thalamic neurons critically supported choice based on current causal relationships.
source: However, while both neuronal populations were found to be important to guide behavior based on current goal value, only thalamic neurons critically supported choice based on current causal relationships.
evidence: This is an inference based on the results from both experiments.

claim: Inhibiting corticothalamic and thalamocortical pathways produced very specific patterns of behavioral alterations, apparent only when no rewards were available.
source: Importantly, inhibiting corticothalamic and thalamocortical pathways produced very specific patterns of behavioral alterations, apparent only when no rewards were available.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of results across different test conditions.

claim: Deficits from pathway inhibition only appeared during tests conducted under extinction conditions.
source: Thus, deficits only appeared during tests conducted under extinction conditions, suggesting that functional interactions between cortical and thalamic areas are important to guide behavior based on the current content of mental representations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of results across different test conditions.

claim: Functional interactions between cortical and thalamic areas are important to guide behavior based on the current content of mental representations.
source: Thus, deficits only appeared during tests conducted under extinction conditions, suggesting that functional interactions between cortical and thalamic areas are important to guide behavior based on the current content of mental representations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of results showing deficits only during extinction tests.

claim: Inhibition of the corticothalamic pathway left the ability to guide choice based on current action-outcome contingency unaltered.
source: Even then, inhibition of the corticothalamic pathway left the ability to guide choice based on current action-outcome contingency unaltered.
evidence: This is an inference based on the results from Experiment 2.

claim: CNO injections alone did not alter instrumental behavior at any stage of the task.
source: Importantly, control experiments showed that CNO injections alone did not alter instrumental behavior at any stage of the task (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is supported by control experiment data provided in the appendix.

claim: The absence of effects of CNO on consumption is sufficient to rule out any non-specific impact of CNO.
source: Together with the absence of effects of CNO on consumption (Figures 3C and 4C), this appears to be sufficient to rule out any non-specific impact of CNO, e.g. due to clozapine conversion (Gomez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the control data and consumption test results.

claim: Projections-defined thalamic and cortical neurons play a specific role in cognitive processes that are necessary when the task includes unobservable information.
source: But more importantly, it points to a specific role for projections-defined thalamic and cortical neurons in cognitive processes that are necessary when the task includes unobservable information (Bradfield et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the overall pattern of results, supported by a citation.

claim: Recent studies have emphasized a consistent role for thalamic nuclei to sustain cortical activity when holding online information is important for subsequent choice.
source: Recent studies have emphasized a consistent role for thalamic nuclei to sustain cortical activity when holding online information is important for subsequent choice (Bolkan et al., 2017; Schmitt et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Only dmPFC-projecting MD neurons were found to be important to support choice based on the current mental representation of action-outcome contingency.
source: The present data support this view as only dmPFC-projecting MD neurons were found to be important to support choice based on the current mental representation of action-outcome contingency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the results from Experiment 1.

claim: MD-lesioned monkeys are unable to persist in successful strategies.
source: Similarly, recent findings obtained in primate suggested that MD-lesioned monkeys are unable to persist in successful strategies (Chakraborty et al., 2016), hinting at a similar problem of maintaining an accurate representation of the associative structure of the current task over time.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a primate study.

claim: The role of the dmPFC in goal-directed actions is now well established.
source: The role of the dmPFC in goal-directed actions is now well established (Corbit and Balleine, 2003; Killcross and Coutureau, 2003; Tran-Tu-Yen et al., 2009; Hart and Balleine, 2016), and is crucial for the acquisition of instrumental action-outcome associations (Tran-Tu-Yen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The dmPFC is crucial for the acquisition of instrumental action-outcome associations.
source: The role of the dmPFC in goal-directed actions is now well established (Corbit and Balleine, 2003; Killcross and Coutureau, 2003; Tran-Tu-Yen et al., 2009; Hart and Balleine, 2016), and is crucial for the acquisition of instrumental action-outcome associations (Tran-Tu-Yen et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Following acquisition, the role of the dmPFC in adapting instrumental responses to contingency changes appears complex, depending on the accessibility of the reward and the nature of contingency changes.
source: However, following acquisition, the role of the dmPFC in adapting instrumental responses to contingency changes appears complex, depending on the accessibility of the reward (Corbit and Balleine, 2003) and the nature of contingency changes (Coutureau et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

source: Interestingly, this last feature is reminiscent from classic studies showing lower levels of instrumental performance in rats sustaining MD lesions (Corbit et al., 2003).

claim: It seems unlikely that low levels of performance alone could account for the specific impairments during devaluation tests because CNO-treated rats exhibited normal extinction.
source: It seems unlikely that low levels of performance alone could account for the specific impairments during devaluation tests because CNO-treated rats exhibited normal extinction at this occasion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of extinction dynamics.

claim: The impairments during devaluation tests could result from an inability to select the correct option in the absence of the sensory feedback provided by the reward.
source: In experiment 1 in particular, CNO-treated rats behave as if they were generalizing but this could result from an inability to select the correct option in the absence of the sensory feedback provided by the reward.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the behavioral results.

claim: The identification of a specific role for corticothalamic projections strongly argues against the view of a thalamus acting only as a relay.
source: The identification of a specific role for corticothalamic projections not only strongly argues against the view of a thalamus acting only as a relay, but also suggests a specific role for these pathways in cognition (Crandall et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results, supported by citations.

claim: Corticothalamic pathways have a specific role in cognition.
source: The identification of a specific role for corticothalamic projections not only strongly argues against the view of a thalamus acting only as a relay, but also suggests a specific role for these pathways in cognition (Crandall et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results, supported by citations.

claim: Conceptual views posit that corticothalamic pathways may contribute to cortical functioning by enabling transthalamic communication between cortical areas.
source: Understanding the functional relevance of these corticothalamic pathways is an important issue as conceptual views posit that they may contribute to cortical functioning by enabling transthalamic communication between cortical areas, thus offering supplemental integrative opportunities (Sherman and Guillery, 2011; Sherman, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: The functional contribution of thalamocortical pathways appears to be consistent with a general role of the thalamus to direct attention toward task's elements relevant for successful performance.
source: The functional contribution of thalamocortical pathways appears to be consistent with that of a general role of the thalamus to direct attention toward task's elements relevant for successful performance (Wolff et al., 2015a; Wolff et al., 2015b), not only in the presence of cues, but also when using the current content of mental representation is required for successful performance.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current results to previous theoretical work via citations.

claim: The directionality of the functional exchanges within neural circuits is one of their fundamental features.
source: These results highlight the directionality of the functional exchanges within neural circuits as one of their fundamental features (see also Bolkan et al., 2017; Lichtenberg et al., 2017), which calls for a more systematic functional assessment of reciprocally connected pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results, supported by citations to related work.

claim: Past research has indicated a time-limited role for both the dmPFC and the MD in the acquisition of goal-directed behaviors.
source: Past research has indicated a time-limited role for both the dmPFC (Ostlund and Balleine, 2005; Tran-Tu-Yen et al., 2009) and the MD (Ostlund and Balleine, 2008) in the acquisition of goal-directed behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Studies that have directly examined functional interactions between cortical and thalamic areas have generally used permanent interventions.
source: While studies that have directly examined functional interactions between cortical and thalamic areas have generally used permanent interventions (Bradfield et al., 2013; Browning et al., 2015), as was the case in the present study, proceeding to stage-limited interventions appears as a valuable prospect to further refine the functional contribution of projections-defined neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology used in previous research, supported by citations.
